title: What is known about 1RB0LF_1LC0LA_1RA0RD_---1RE_1LA1RC_0LB0RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LF_1LC0LA_1RA0RD_---1RE_1LA1RC_0LB0RC.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine was one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. It does not halt from blank tape: Lean proves it, with a symbolic checker that the kernel proves sound, the round trips evaluated by the kernel and the long runs by compiled code (native_decide). This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: It never halts. Lean proves nonhalting: from blank tape the machine reaches one of 62 tape templates and moves from template to template forever. The 62 round trips are checked by the kernel; the start and the 62 ends of an epoch (2.5 million symbolic moves) by native_decide.

What it does. Each time B reaches the left end the tape reads B> 00 (01)a 000 (01)b 000 …, a list of counts separated by short words. The rightward sweep turns 010101 into 011001 and the leftward sweep turns it back. Each round trip takes 3 from a, while the end of the list runs through one of four periodic patterns (periods 15, 22, 16 and 9 round trips) and b gains 99, 141, 99 or 57 per period. When a is used up, b takes its place and a new, longer epoch begins: the first counts of successive epochs are 4, 12, 20, 38, 68, 122, 240, 484, 1002, 2104, 4375, ….

Why it cannot halt. Only D reading a 0 halts, after C>1 0. Every round trip of every pattern and every way an epoch can end has been checked as a symbolic run with the counts as variables, and each lands on a template again; a potential on the counts shows that an epoch always ends with the second count large enough for those runs.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 39,660 cells have been visited and 19,822 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.497). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.507).

claims.title: Shift rules
claims.text: B with a 1 behind it turns each 010101 into 011001 going right (14 steps a copy); C with 110 ahead turns each 011001 back into 010101 going left (22 steps a copy).

claims.title: The halting situations
claims.text: C>1 0 halts after one step, E>1 1 0 and F>1 1 0 after two, D>1 1 1 0 after three.

claims.title: A verified symbolic checker
claims.text: lean/SymCheck.lean: configurations whose tape is a list of cells and runs wn with n linear in some variables; auto finds the moves itself (a run crossed by a shift rule found on the spot, else one step) and compares normal forms at the left end. auto_reach proves that a successful check means the machine makes that run, for every value of the variables.

claims.title: The 62 round trips
claims.text: Each phase template B> 00 (01)3k+4 000 (01)3j+β rest at [k+1, j] reaches the next phase at [k, j + dj] (200 to 2,500 symbolic moves each), evaluated by the kernel. The tables also show that j + 2k + pot never decreases in a round and is at least 215 after an epoch.

claims.title: The 62 ends of an epoch
claims.text: Each template at [0, j+200] reaches a template again, with the old second count as the new first (4,200 to 127,000 symbolic moves each, 2.5 million in all), evaluated by compiled code; the kernel runs out of memory on runs this long.

claims.title: The start
claims.text: From blank tape the machine reaches template 31 (pattern R1, phase 16) with first count 118 and second 496, at step 1,277,431 (147,895 symbolic moves).

claims.title: It does not halt from blank tape
claims.text: The invariant “at a template with j + 2k + pot ≥ 215” holds at the start and is restored after a round or an end, each taking at least one step, so the run is defined for every length. #print axioms lists propext, Quot.sound and the two native_decide axioms.

claims.title: Four regimes, growing epochs
claims.text: How the templates were found: along the run, the list at the left end settles each epoch into one of four periodic patterns of period 15, 22, 16 or 9 round trips, in which the first count drops by 3 per trip and the second grows by 99, 141, 99 or 57 per period. Concrete simulations from every phase and residue return to a pattern.

claims.title: D never reads a 0 in 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps
claims.text: In the first 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps the machine is in state D 22,202,037 times, every time on a 1: the halting transition D0 is never close to firing in a way the run shows.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RD_1RC0LF_1LA0LB_---1RE_1LB1RA_0LC0RA up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: It never halts, and Lean proves it: the tape is a list of counts, the first one counts down by 3 on every trip, the rest of the list cycles through one of four patterns, and every way this can go has been checked symbolically. This page runs it in your browser and shows the counters.

facts.text: Proved in Lean; the 62 round trips by the kernel, the start and the 62 epoch ends by native_decide.
No halt in the C simulator; 39,660 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: The whole argument in one picture
html: This page walks through the Lean proof that this machine, started on a blank tape, never halts. You do not need to know Lean or Turing machine theory. Each step says what is claimed, shows it on the real machine in your browser, and says what checks it: Kernel means Lean's small trusted core checked it; native_decide means Lean ran a compiled program and trusts that the compiler and the runtime computed correctly.
The idea of the proof is an invariant: a description of a set of tapes, called good, with three properties.
• The run reaches a good tape. From the blank tape, after 1,277,431 steps, the tape is good.
• A good tape always leads to another good tape. From any good tape the machine makes at least one step, without halting, and arrives at a good tape again.
• So the machine never halts. Repeating step 2 forever gives runs of every length, and a machine that halts has runs of only bounded length.

What makes a tape "good" is the content of the rest of this page: it is one of 62 templates, a list of numbers written on the tape in a fixed pattern, with two of the numbers free (called k and j) and a size condition on them. Step 2 then splits into finitely many checks, one per template and case.

sections.heading: How it could halt, and what the proof has to show
html: The table has one missing entry: D reading a 0. That is the only way to halt. The only transition into D is C reading a 1 (C writes 0, moves right, enters D), so a halt happens exactly when the head in state C sees 1 0.

The proof never looks for this pattern directly. It shows something stronger: from the blank tape, for every number n, the first n steps are all defined. That is the Lean statement ¬ HaltsFromBlank, where HaltsFromBlank means "some step reaches a configuration with no transition".
Press Step to see the halting pattern play out on a made-up tape.

sections.heading: The tape is a list of numbers
html: Watch the machine for a while (the simulator above) and most of the tape turns out to be long stretches of 0 1 0 1 0 1 …. Stop it at the moments when the head, in state B, stands at the left end of the written tape on a 0. At those moments the tape always reads
B>00(01) × a000(01) × b000(01) × c…

a list of numbers a, b, c, … written as stretches of 01, separated by short words such as 000, 00001000 or 11. The machine is a little computer working on this list. The first number a counts down, the second number b grows, and the short tail after them goes round in a cycle.
Below is the real tape at step 1,277,431, computed in your browser from the blank tape. Each blue or green bar is one stretch of 01, with its count.

sections.heading: Crossing a stretch: the shift rules
html: Between turns the head sweeps across the long stretches. A stretch of a million cells would take a million steps to simulate, but what happens to it is simple, and Lean proves it once for every length:
• Going right (sweep_right): B, with a 1 just behind it, turns each block 010101 into 011001 and comes out the other side, again in state B, after exactly 14 steps per block.
• Going left (sweep_left): C, with 110 ahead of it, turns each 011001 back into 010101, 22 steps per block.

Each is proved by running one block for real (rfl, so Lean's kernel computes the 14 or 22 steps) and then a general lemma, cross_r or cross_l, that says: if one copy takes the head through in the same state, n copies do too, in n times the steps. Kernel

sections.heading: One round trip, for any size
html: From one left-end moment to the next is a round trip: the head sweeps right to the far end of the tape and back. What it does to the list depends on the short tail, which takes one of 62 shapes (the 62 templates, named R0_0 … R3_8, see the next step). In each template the first two numbers are written with two free variables:
a = 3k + 4    b = 3j + β   (β between 6 and 8, fixed per template)

Lean proves, for each template t and for every k and j: a round trip takes template t with numbers (k + 1, j) to the next template with numbers (k, j + dj), where dj is a small constant listed for each template. So a drops by 3 and b grows by 3·dj. These are the 62 theorems round_0 … round_61. Kernel

Try it: pick a template and small values of k and j, and run one round trip on the real machine. The diagram shows the tape (rows are moments, time going down; dark = 1) and the path of the head (orange line): out to the right end over the stretches, and back. The check at the bottom compares the tape after the trip with what the theorem predicts, cell by cell.

sections.heading: 62 templates in four cycles
html: Follow the templates from one round trip to the next and they go round in cycles. There are four cycles, called regimes R0 to R3, with 15, 22, 16 and 9 templates. After one full lap of a regime the tail is exactly as it was, a has dropped by 45, 66, 48 or 27 (3 per trip), and b has grown by 99, 141, 99 or 57. Click a template in the rings to see its shape.
Template R0_0 as Lean states it (dashed bars: counts with variables):
One lap of the selected regime, as observed in the run (a and b are concrete numbers here):

sections.heading: When the countdown runs out: from one epoch to the next
html: Round trips need k ≥ 1. When k reaches 0 (a = 4) the countdown cannot go on. What happens next has three parts, and Lean checks them together as one end case per template. We call the stretch between two such events an epoch.

• The reset (three returns to the left end). The last 4 copies of 01 in a are used up and the short word in front of b is rewritten. The old b ends up first in the list, with a few more copies. In the example below the new a is 724 + 6 = 730.

• The transient (up to about 145 round trips). Each trip still takes 3 from the new a, as before. But the tail of the list is in disorder after the reset, so it does not yet follow any of the 62 templates. The new b starts small and grows. Now and then two pieces of the tail merge.
• Settling. The tail falls into one of the four regimes, and the tape is a template again: endT t, with a new k that is large and a new j that is small.

Lean proves, for each template t and every j: from template t with numbers (0, j + 200), the machine reaches the template endT t with numbers (j + endC1, endC2). These are the 62 end cases, checked together as ends_ok. native_decide

The first epoch end of the proof, in the real run. At step 1,908,405 the tape is template R1_10 with k = 0 and j = 239 (a = 4, b = 724). The proof's end case for R1_10 says the run reaches R1_16 with k = (239 − 200) + 81 = 120 and j = 259. Below, the browser runs the machine through it, from that step to step 4,054,968. The slider moves through every moment at which the head is back at the left end. The chart shows a (blue) and b (green) at each of those moments.
<svg class="pw-chart" id="pw-ep1chart" viewBox="0 0 760 240" role="img" aria-label="a and b at each left-end moment during the first epoch end"></svg>
The reset, moment by moment. The four left-end moments from step 1,908,405 to step 1,946,128, as lists. Blue is the first count, green the second.

Why "j + 200". During the transient the new a, which comes from the old b, still loses 3 every round trip. It must not run out before the tail has settled, or the end case would be a different computation. The symbolic checker cannot ask whether a count is zero, so it needs a guarantee up front. The end cases are stated for an old b of at least 3 · 200 + β copies (j ≥ 200). The longest transient takes under 150 round trips, so it uses fewer than 450 of those copies. Step 7 shows that j is always at least 200 when an epoch ends.

The button runs all 62 end cases on the real machine at the smallest size the proof allows (j = 200 exactly), and checks that each reaches its predicted template cell for cell. This is an independent check of the claims behind ends_ok, at one size. Lean's check covers every size. The chart shows how many left-end moments each end case takes.

Epoch after epoch. In a round trip b grows by roughly 2.2 for every 1 that a loses, and at the reset b becomes the new a. So each epoch is about twice as long as the one before. The chart shows the first number a at the start of each epoch, read off the certificate's tables starting from the template the run reaches at step 1,277,431 (log scale).

sections.heading: Before the first template: the setup
html: The proof starts at step 1,277,431, not at step 0. The first 1,277,431 steps are the setup, and Lean checks them as one long computation: start_ok runs the symbolic checker from the blank tape to template R1_16 with k = 38, j = 163. The sweep rules let it cross long stretches in one move, so that takes about 148,000 symbolic moves. native_decide

What happens in the setup? The machine does the same things as later, at small sizes. From the start the left-end list counts down a by 3 per round trip, and resets when a runs out. So the setup is a series of short epochs (the table below lists their resets), each roughly twice as long as the one before. In the early ones the numbers are too small for the tail to settle into a regime. The first time the tape fits one of the 62 templates is step 1,277,431, in the epoch that began at step 503,461. That is where the proof takes over.

The chart shows a (blue) and b (green) at every left-end moment from the blank tape to step 4,054,968, computed in your browser (log scale; dots mark the resets). Use the slider to see the list at each moment.
<svg class="pw-chart" id="pw-setchart" viewBox="0 0 760 260" role="img" aria-label="a and b at each left-end moment from blank tape"></svg>

The table lists each reset of the setup and of the first proof epoch: the step, b at the last moment before the reset, and the new a just after it. The new a is the old b plus some copies: 6 at the first reset of the proof, more during the setup, where pieces of the tail also merge into it.

sections.heading: Why there is always enough room
html: The end cases need j ≥ 200 at the moment k reaches 0. The proof gets this from a potential, a single number that never goes down too far:
where pot(t) is a number between 0 and 15 listed for each template. Two facts about the tables, both checked by Lean's kernel (tables_ok) Kernel:
<dt>in a round trip</dt><dd>k drops by 1 (Φ loses 2), j grows by dj, and pot changes; the tables satisfy pot(t) + 2 ≤ pot(next) + dj, so Φ never decreases.</dd>
<dt>after an epoch end</dt><dd>the new values give Φ ≥ endC2 + 2·endC1 + pot(endT) ≥ 215 for every template.</dd>

So Φ ≥ 215 on every good tape. At an epoch end k = 0, so j ≥ 215 − pot(t) ≥ 215 − 15 = 200, exactly what the end cases need. The chart follows Φ along the first rounds of the run, from the tables (log scale; the dashed line is 215).

sections.heading: How Lean checks every size at once
html: A round trip from template t at (k + 1, j) is a claim about infinitely many tapes, one for each k and j. Lean cannot simulate them one by one. Instead it runs the machine symbolically: the tape is a list of tokens, single cells and stretches (01)^n whose count n is a formula such as 3k + 7.
Template R0_0 at (k + 1, j), as the checker sees it:

The checker steps the machine on cells it can see. When the head meets a stretch with a formula count, it simulates one copy on its own (as in Step 2) and, if the head comes out the far side in the same state, crosses the whole stretch at once. If it would need to know whether a count is 0 or not, it gives up and the check fails.

The checker is a program, auto in lean/SymCheck.lean, and it comes with a theorem, auto_reach, proved once by the kernel: if auto answers true for a start and a target, then for every value of the variables the real machine goes from the start to the target in at least one step. So each round trip becomes a computation: "does auto answer true on this input?". The trip takes 200 to 2,500 symbolic moves. Kernel
Who runs that computation is the one place where the proof uses two levels of trust:
<dt>decide +kernel</dt><dd>Lean's kernel evaluates the program itself, step by step. This is the most trusted way, and it is used for the 62 round trips and the potential tables.</dd>

<dt>native_decide</dt><dd>Lean compiles the program to machine code and runs it. The kernel then accepts the answer as an axiom. Used for the start (about 148,000 symbolic moves) and the 62 end cases (2.5 million in all), because the kernel ran out of memory (over 6 GB) on runs that long.</dd>

sections.heading: What rests on native_decide, and how else it was checked
html: Every piece of the proof, and what it rests on. A wrong number anywhere in the tables cannot make the proof pass: it would only make one of the checks answer false.
Machine.leanthe machine's table and what a step is (generated from the machine's name)Kernel
sweep_right, sweep_leftthe two shift rules, for any number of blocksKernel
auto_reachthe symbolic checker agrees with the real machineKernel
round_0 … round_61the 62 round trips, every k and jKernel
tables_okthe potential never lets j fall below 200 at an epoch endKernel
start_okblank tape reaches template R1_16 at (38, 163)native_decide
ends_okthe 62 epoch ends, every jnative_decide
nonhaltingglues the pieces together (the induction of the first picture)Kernel

#print axioms H36670.nonhalting lists propext and Quot.sound (two standard axioms of Lean's logic) and exactly two native_decide axioms, one for start_ok and one for ends_ok. Trusting them means trusting that Lean's compiler and runtime evaluated the checker correctly on those inputs. The checker's own logic is not trusted: auto_reach is a kernel proof.

Independent checks of the two native_decide pieces Computed. These are separate from Lean and do not replace a kernel proof, but they test the same claims by a different route, plain simulation with a small C program:
• The start: the plain simulation reaches exactly template R1_16 at (38, 163) at step 1,277,431. You can repeat it above in Step 1; your browser does the same computation.
• The 62 end cases: each one was run concretely at j = 0 (b with exactly 3·200 + β copies) and at j = 13, and each reached exactly the predicted template and numbers, taking up to 2.6 million steps.
• The whole chain: the sequence of templates the tables predict was matched, in order, against the plain run from blank tape: 2,765 consecutive good tapes up to step 3·108, including 4 epoch ends.

A proof using only the kernel needs the long runs cut into pieces of a few thousand symbolic moves, with each intermediate tape written out (about 900 pieces). That work was started and is not finished.

sections.heading: The last lines of the proof, in words
html: The end of lean/Cert.lean, theorem by theorem:
<dt>Good c</dt><dd>c is template t with numbers k, j (t one of the 62), and j + 2k + pot(t) ≥ 215.</dd>

start_good
some run from the blank tape ends at a good tape (from start_ok).

<dt>good_step</dt><dd>from a good tape, at least one step leads to a good tape. If k ≥ 1 it uses that template's round trip, if k = 0 its end case, and the tables to show the new tape is good again.</dd>

nonhalting_of
by induction on N: for every N there is a run from blank of length at least N ending at a good tape. So runs of every length exist (not_halts_of_forall, forall_of_unbounded), and the machine does not halt.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.497). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.507).
After 109 steps the tape spans 39,660 cells (8,102 left of the start, 19,554 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is described above.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB0RD_1RC0LF_1LA0LB_---1RE_1LB1RA_0LC0RA: rename A→B, B→C, C→A, D→D, E→E, F→F; it is this table started in state C

summary: A list of counts written in stretches of 01: each round trip takes 3 from the first count while the rest of the list cycles through one of four periodic patterns, and when the first count runs out the second takes its place; Lean proves it never halts (kernel rounds, native_decide for the long runs).
family: two-sided bouncer, a list of (01)-stretches; four periodic regimes in growing epochs
